# Backpressure

Backpressure is a fundamental mechanism in streaming pipelines that allows a slow downstream consumer to signal an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate. Without backpressure, an unconstrained producer would continue emitting data faster than the consumer can process it, causing an unbounded buffer to grow until the system exhausts available memory.

## Problem

In a typical streaming pipeline, if the producer emits data faster than the consumer can handle, intermediate buffers will accumulate unprocessed items. Without backpressure, this growth is unbounded — the system can crash or become unstable due to memory exhaustion.

## Common Implementation Patterns

Backpressure is implemented in several ways:

### Bounded Queues
The simplest approach: use a queue with a fixed maximum capacity. Once the queue is full, the producer thread blocks (cannot emit more) until the consumer drains some items. This naturally couples producer and consumer rates without explicit coordination.

### Credit-Based Flow Control
The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send a specific number of items (a "credit"). Once the producer exhausts its credit, it must wait for the consumer to grant more. This decouples producer and consumer threads while maintaining rate control.

### Reactive-Pull Models
Rather than the producer pushing data to the consumer, the consumer pulls items on its own schedule. The producer only generates data when explicitly requested, naturally aligning emission to consumption rate.
